      Rendering & Feature Showcase
This page exists to be looked at. Everything okf-loom can render lives below, and because you are (probably) viewing it in the live studio, everything above this line — the type band, aliases subtitle, entity chips, typed relations, provenance, and citations — came from the frontmatter, not the body.
Try this while you read: select any sentence on this page and a Comment button appears. The graph icon in the top bar shows how this page connects to the rest of the bundle.
Text and structure
Standard Markdown works the way you expect: bold, italic, inline code, and internal links that get hover previews — rest your pointer on that link. External links open in a new tab.
Ordered listsWith nesting
Unordered childrenAs deep as you needAnd back out again
Tables
Every table is interactive: click a header to sort (numbers, dates, and currency sort numerically), drag a header's right edge to resize the column, and on longer tables a toolbar adds a row filter and a Copy CSV button. Column alignment follows the GFM separator row (:---, :---:, ---:).

Showing a read-only view. docs-bundle 31 concepts6 types390 links Explore the graph okf-loom Documentation okf-loom is a GitHub-cloneable, vendor-neutral, harness-agnostic skill repository with a documentation bundle, focused resources, and checkout-local scripts. It validates, searches, discovers gaps in, updates, and renders a navigable wiki + graph viewer for any Open Knowledge Format bundle. See the current okf-loom specification; upstream OKF SPEC v0.1 remains the base wire-format reference. See it in action: the Rendering & Feature Showcase packs every renderer (Mermaid, KaTeX, syntax highlighting, tables) and live feature onto one page. This bundle IS okf-loom's own documentation, organised in the Diátaxis framework: each concept belongs to one of four content types, and the type tells you how to read it. Demo Rendering & Feature Showcase — every renderer (Mermaid, KaTeX, syntax highlighting, tables) and every governed key on one page. Open it first when evaluating the viewer. Four kinds of documentation Learning Walk-throughs written for someone new to okf-loom. Read top to bottom; reproduce every step. id=\"okf-loom-architecture\"\u003eokf-loom architecture\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis essay explains the \u003cem\u003erationale\u003c/em\u003e behind okf-loom's shape. It is the why, not the what: the neutral module-by-module walkthrough lives in the deep \u003ca href=\"/reference/architecture.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/reference/architecture.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e, and the per-command surface lives in \u003ca href=\"/reference/cli.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003ecli.md\u003c/a\u003e. Read this when you have used okf-loom and are wondering why it is organised the way it is.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eokf-loom mirrors the format's philosophy: it is \u003cstrong\u003epermissive\u003c/strong\u003e (load never hard-fails on soft issues), \u003cstrong\u003elayered\u003c/strong\u003e (a cheap core with optional extras), and \u003cstrong\u003esingle-source-of-truth\u003c/strong\u003e (one canonical model every consumer reads). Those three properties fall out of a small number of deliberate structural choices, which this essay walks through.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-founding-lesson-one-canonical-model\"\u003eThe founding lesson: one canonical model\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe single most important idea in okf-loom is borrowed from Quartz (see \u003ca href=\"/explanation/research.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/explanation/research.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e §1): \u003cstrong\u003eone canonical content index feeds many features.\u003c/strong\u003e Do not build a separate index per consumer; emit one graph-plus-document model and let every consumer read it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eIn okf-loom that model is the \u003ccode\u003eContentIndex\u003c/code\u003e. It is computed lazily from the loaded \u003ccode\u003eBundle\u003c/code\u003e and memoised on the bundle instance, so it is built once and reused by everything that needs it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"mermaid\"\u003eflowchart TB\n    Disk[(\"disk (.md files)\")]\n    Load[\"Bundle.load(root)\u0026lt;br/\u0026gt;\u0026lt;i\u0026gt;parse frontmatter + headings only\u0026lt;/i\u0026gt;\"]\n    CI[\"Bundle.content_index()\"]\n    Model[(\"ContentIndex\u0026lt;br/\u0026gt;\u0026lt;i\u0026gt;one canonical model\u0026lt;/i\u0026gt;\")]\n    Validate[\"validate_bundle\u0026lt;br/\u0026gt;discover_suggestions\"]\n    Search[\"search_bundle\u0026lt;br/\u0026gt;(6 modes)\"]\n    Viewer[\"viewer\u0026lt;br/\u0026gt;(serve / build / render)\"]\n\n    Disk --\u0026gt; Load --\u0026gt; CI --\u0026gt; Model\n    Model --\u0026gt; Validate\n    Model --\u0026gt; Search\n    Model --\u0026gt; Viewer\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree properties fall out of this:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCheap to load.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eBundle.load\u003c/code\u003e parses frontmatter and headings; it does not build the graph or the content index. Those are computed on first call and memoised. A thousand-concept bundle loads in well under a second.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNo second index for the viewer.\u003c/strong\u003e Search, graph, listings, and the viewer all read the same in-memory object. There is never a drift bug where the viewer shows one graph and search assumes another.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMutations are round-trip.\u003c/strong\u003e Every writer goes through \u003ccode\u003eparse_document → modify → serialize_document\u003c/code\u003e, so unknown frontmatter keys and key order survive editing. The model and the file never disagree.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe reason this matters is drift. In a system with a search index, a graph cache, and a render cache, each one is a chance for the user to see stale data after a change. Collapsing all of them onto one model removes an entire class of bugs by construction.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"one-model-three-render-targets\"\u003eOne model, three render targets\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe viewer does not have one shape; it has three, all driven by the same canonical \u003ccode\u003eContentIndex\u003c/code\u003e. This is the Quartz lesson applied to the deployment shapes OKF wants to support — portability, interactivity, embedding in a harness, and \u003ccode\u003efile://\u003c/code\u003e-openable artefacts.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eTarget\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eCommand\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eWhen it is the right choice\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eLive HTTP server\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom serve \u0026lt;bundle\u0026gt;\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eThe authoring loop. Watches files; live reload; harness embedding points a browser at the URL.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eMulti-file static site\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom build --target {spa,static}\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA published reading experience (\u003ccode\u003espa\u003c/code\u003e) or server-rendered, JS-optional, printable, SEO-friendly HTML (\u003ccode\u003estatic\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eSelf-contained single file\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom render \u0026lt;bundle\u0026gt;\u003c/code\u003e (or \u003ccode\u003ebuild --target single-file\u003c/code\u003e)\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eOne portable HTML — email it, \u003ccode\u003efile://\u003c/code\u003e-open it, attach it to a ticket. Embeds the bundle as JSON.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe same model, three projections. The deep comparison of these patterns (and why each one earns its place) is in \u003ca href=\"/explanation/research.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/explanation/research.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e §15; the recipes for the build targets are in \u003ca href=\"/how-to/build_static_site.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eBuild a static site\u003c/a\u003e and the embedding shape is in \u003ca href=\"/how-to/embed_in_harness.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eEmbed the viewer in an agent harness\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe single-file target is intentionally \u003cem\u003eone export option\u003c/em\u003e, not the only viewer. It re-encodes the whole bundle into one file, which is great for sharing and bad for large bundles. Treating it as the sole surface would have made okf-loom useless past a few hundred concepts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-the-modules-have-their-shapes\"\u003eWhy the modules have their shapes\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eokf-loom is a flat set of focused modules rather than a framework. Each one owns one concern and exposes it through a small, stable function surface. The module map lives in \u003ca href=\"/reference/architecture.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/reference/architecture.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e; the \u003cem\u003ewhy\u003c/em\u003e for each is below.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"the-parse-model-core\"\u003eThe parse / model core\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003eparse.py\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003emodel.py\u003c/code\u003e are the floor everything stands on. Parsing is deliberately \u003cem\u003elazy and forgiving\u003c/em\u003e: frontmatter is parsed with \u003ccode\u003eyaml.safe_load\u003c/code\u003e, links are extracted in both forms plus wikilinks, and nothing in the load path raises on a soft issue. A concept with a broken link, a missing description, or an unknown type still loads; it just accumulates warnings from the validator.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is a direct reflection of SPEC §9 — conformance is the three hard rules, and everything else is guidance. A loader that rejected soft issues would be a stricter gate than the spec itself imposes, which would defeat the format's \"never reject knowledge\" posture.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"validate-the-conformance-oracle\"\u003eValidate: the conformance oracle\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003evalidate.py\u003c/code\u003e is shaped as an oracle that returns a structured report, not a linter that exits. Findings split into \u003ccode\u003eerrors\u003c/code\u003e (the SPEC §9 hard rules), \u003ccode\u003ewarnings\u003c/code\u003e, and \u003ccode\u003einfo\u003c/code\u003e, and the same report is consumed by the CLI (\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom validate\u003c/code\u003e, with \u003ccode\u003e--strict\u003c/code\u003e for CI), by the live studio (which validates before every agent write so an unparseable file is never persisted), and by the discovery pass (which re-surfaces broken links).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eValidation profiles (\u003ccode\u003espec\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eproducer\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eloose\u003c/code\u003e) remap severities so one validator serves a spec reader, a producer-side CI, and a migration aid without changing the wire format. See \u003ca href=\"/reference/cli.md#validate\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003ecli.md\u003c/a\u003e for the flags.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"discover-and-plan-the-gap-finders\"\u003eDiscover and plan: the gap-finders\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003ediscover.py\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003eplan.py\u003c/code\u003e exist because a graph of plain links will always have gaps, and the agent's job is to close them. Discovery emits structured \u003cem\u003esuggestions\u003c/em\u003e (rule, severity, message, target concept); planning turns those suggestions (plus stale indexes and unmirrored typed relations) into a \u003cem\u003ereviewable, executable action envelope\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe split between the two is deliberate. Discovery is cheap and runs over the whole bundle; planning is the layer that decides which suggestions are mechanical (carry a runnable \u003ccode\u003eargv\u003c/code\u003e) and which need an agent judgement (carry an \u003ccode\u003eargv_template\u003c/code\u003e with placeholders, a confidence score, and an instruction). Both can be scoped to a single concept and its neighbours, which is what makes per-change enrichment fast — see \u003ca href=\"/how-to/discover_and_fix_gaps.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eDiscover and fix gaps\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"update-the-round-trip-safe-mutator\"\u003eUpdate: the round-trip-safe mutator\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003eupdate.py\u003c/code\u003e is where the \"mutations are round-trip\" property is enforced. Every op kind (\u003ccode\u003eadd_link\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eadd_tag\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eset_frontmatter\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eadd_relation\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eappend_body_section\u003c/code\u003e, …) goes through the same \u003ccode\u003eparse_document → modify → serialize_document\u003c/code\u003e pipeline, so frontmatter key order and unknown keys survive. All writes are atomic (tmp + rename), and the ops are idempotent — re-applying the same plan reports \u003ccode\u003eapplied:0, skipped:N\u003c/code\u003e with reasons.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eIn the live studio, \u003ccode\u003eupdate.apply_plan\u003c/code\u003e accepts \u003ccode\u003estudio\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eactor\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eorigin\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003egroup_id\u003c/code\u003e and threads them through every op, so a multi-op pass is one group-undoable unit. That threading is what makes the change list exact and undo complete.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"the-viewer-and-its-overrides\"\u003eThe viewer and its overrides\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe viewer is a thin server-rendered HTML layer over \u003ccode\u003eContentIndex\u003c/code\u003e, with five override surfaces that let a bundle customise rendering without forking: template overrides, static-asset overrides, a type palette, a viewer config file, and a \u003ccode\u003eViewerPlugin\u003c/code\u003e hook. Crucially, the plugin hook is gated behind a \u003cstrong\u003etwo-layer active-code gate\u003c/strong\u003e — a bundle must declare \u003ccode\u003eviewer.allow_active_code: true\u003c/code\u003e \u003cem\u003eand\u003c/em\u003e the operator must pass \u003ccode\u003e--allow-active-code\u003c/code\u003e — because a plugin runs code in the user's browser, and a downloaded bundle should never silently do that.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is okf-loom's distinction between \u003cem\u003edata safety\u003c/em\u003e (always on, invisible) and \u003cem\u003eactive code\u003c/em\u003e (opt-in, explicit). Editing, saving, and watching are never behind the active-code gate; running a bundle's JavaScript always is.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"the-studio-the-collaboration-layer\"\u003eThe studio: the collaboration layer\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003estudio.py\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003ewatch.py\u003c/code\u003e are the live layer that turns \u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom serve\u003c/code\u003e into a live collaborative studio. The studio's defining structural choice is the \u003cstrong\u003esingle internal write funnel\u003c/strong\u003e: every concept write — from a CLI mutator, from \u003ccode\u003eapply_plan\u003c/code\u003e, from \u003ccode\u003ePOST /__apply\u003c/code\u003e, from \u003ccode\u003ePOST /__undo\u003c/code\u003e — goes through one function, \u003ccode\u003eStudio.save_concept\u003c/code\u003e. That is what makes every write attributed, undoable, and visible on the change list with no duplicated bookkeeping between the CLI and HTTP paths.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe full rationale for the studio's shape — comment-driven directing, no review gate, all-on defaults, the separate archive track, the trust model — is its own essay in \u003ca href=\"live_studio_design.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003elive_studio_design.md\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-flat-modules-instead-of-a-framework\"\u003eWhy flat modules instead of a framework\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA recurring design choice is that okf-loom is a flat checkout of focused modules rather than an opinionated framework you subclass. The reasons are practical:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eEvery module is independently importable.\u003c/strong\u003e You can \u003ccode\u003efrom okf_loom.validate import validate_bundle\u003c/code\u003e without dragging in the viewer, the server, or the studio. A CI runner, a meta-agent's subprocess, and an air-gapped notebook all import only what they need.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThere is no hidden global state.\u003c/strong\u003e The content index is memoised on the \u003ccode\u003eBundle\u003c/code\u003e instance and released when it is garbage-collected; \u003ccode\u003eBundle.invalidate()\u003c/code\u003e resets the caches. A long-running server that reloads bundles does not accumulate stale state.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eExtension points are explicit, not magical.\u003c/strong\u003e Five override surfaces for the viewer; a \u003ccode\u003eSearchBackend\u003c/code\u003e Protocol for search; a capability registry for optional format extensions; a module-level \u003ccode\u003e_RULES\u003c/code\u003e dict for discovery rules. Adding behaviour means adding a function and registering it, not subclassing a base.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe cost of this choice is that there is no \"plugin lifecycle\" with fancy hooks; if you want rich server-side behaviour you wire it into your own code by checking \u003ccode\u003eresolved.is_active(\"...\")\u003c/code\u003e on the capability registry. okf-loom judges that a fair trade for staying harness-agnostic and free of magic.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"forward-compatibility-as-an-architectural-property\"\u003eForward compatibility as an architectural property\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe last architectural choice worth naming is that \u003cstrong\u003eforward compatibility is structural, not bolted on.\u003c/strong\u003e Four mechanisms carry it:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSpec-version tracking.\u003c/strong\u003e A single \u003ccode\u003eSPEC_VERSION\u003c/code\u003e constant; a bundle's declared \u003ccode\u003eokf_version\u003c/code\u003e is read on load and a mismatch produces a warning and best-effort consumption, never a hard failure (SPEC §11 mandate).\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCapability registry.\u003c/strong\u003e Optional behaviours live behind named capabilities (\u003ccode\u003eokf.cap.typed_relations\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eokf.cap.entities\u003c/code\u003e, …) that are \u003cem\u003erecognised-if-present, never required\u003c/em\u003e. A bundle opts in by using the governed keys. See \u003ca href=\"/reference/capabilities.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003ecapabilities.md\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMigration hooks.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom upgrade --check\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003e--apply\u003c/code\u003e runs idempotent transformers reusing the same parse-modify-serialize pipeline. No migrations are defined for v0.1 because it is the baseline.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMarker-safe auto-update.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e regeneration never destroys hand-authored content — it skips hand-authored files, rewrites only inside \u003ccode\u003e\u0026lt;!-- okf:generated:index begin/end --\u0026gt;\u003c/code\u003e markers, or replaces files that declare \u003ccode\u003egenerated: true\u003c/code\u003e. \u003ccode\u003elog.md\u003c/code\u003e is always append-only.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe unifying principle is the SPEC §2 round-trip rule: producers may add any keys; consumers must preserve them. The architecture is shaped so that okf-loom is always a \u003cem\u003econsumer that adds value\u003c/em\u003e (validation, search, rendering, collaboration) and never a \u003cem\u003eproducer that strips information\u003c/em\u003e. That is what lets the format and okf-loom evolve independently.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"see-also\"\u003eSee also\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca survey (Quartz, Obsidian, MkDocs, …) that produced the \"one content index\" lesson.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eReturn to \u003ca href=\"/explanation/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eExplanation\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e", "explanation/diataxis": "\u003ch2 id=\"why-this-bundle-uses-diátaxis\"\u003eWhy this bundle uses Diátaxis\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis bundle is organised by \u003ca href=\"https://diataxis.fr/\" class=\"okf-external\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eDiátaxis\u003c/a\u003e, a documentation framework that sorts content by \u003cem\u003epurpose\u003c/em\u003e rather than by topic. This essay explains why this bundle adopted it, what the four content types are, why mixing them in a single file confuses readers, and how the framework maps cleanly onto OKF's \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e frontmatter key.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eDiátaxis is the source framework; the authoritative explanation lives at \u003ca href=\"https://diataxis.fr/\" class=\"okf-external\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ehttps://diataxis.fr/\u003c/a\u003e. The comparative notes that informed this bundle's adoption are in \u003ca href=\"/explanation/research.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/explanation/research.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e §13.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-problem-diátaxis-solves\"\u003eThe problem Diátaxis solves\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eDocumentation fails in a familiar way: a single page tries to teach a beginner, guide a practitioner, describe a mechanism, and argue a design choice all at once. The beginner drowns in the reference; the practitioner cannot find the recipe for the task at hand; the reader who wants the \u003cem\u003ewhy\u003c/em\u003e is buried under the \u003cem\u003ehow\u003c/em\u003e. The page serves no posture well because it is trying to serve all of them.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eDiátaxis observes that documentation readers are really in one of four postures, and that each posture asks a different question and wants a different kind of answer. The cure is to stop writing one document for all four and start writing one document \u003cem\u003eper posture\u003c/em\u003e, then make it obvious which is which.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-four-content-types-and-their-postures\"\u003eThe four content types and their postures\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eDiátaxis names four content types. Each one pairs a reader posture with a promise the author makes to that reader.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eType\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eReader posture\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eQuestion\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003ePromise the author makes\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTutorial\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eLearning\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cem\u003eHow do I learn this?\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eTakes a beginner by the hand; the reader reproduces every step and arrives at a working result.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow-to guide\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eDoing\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cem\u003eHow do I do this one task?\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eSolves a specific real-world goal; assumes the reader knows the basics and wants a recipe.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eReference\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eFinding\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cem\u003eWhat exactly does the machinery do?\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eDescribes the machinery neutrally; no steps, no opinion, no why.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eExplanation\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eUnderstanding\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cem\u003eWhy is it shaped this way?\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eClarifies the choices, the constraints, the alternatives; discussion, not direction.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe two axes underneath that table matter as much as the cells. The top row (Tutorial, How-to) is \u003cem\u003eaction-oriented\u003c/em\u003e — the reader is trying to do something. The bottom row (Reference, Explanation) is \u003cem\u003ecognition-oriented\u003c/em\u003e — the reader is trying to know something. The left column (Tutorial, Reference) is about the \u003cem\u003etool as it is\u003c/em\u003e; the right column (How-to, Explanation) is about the \u003cem\u003ereader's work and choices\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"mermaid\"\u003equadrantChart\n    title Diátaxis content types\n    x-axis \"Action-oriented\" --\u0026gt; \"Cognition-oriented\"\n    y-axis \"Learning\" --\u0026gt; \"Working\"\n    quadrant-1 Reference\n    quadrant-2 Explanation\n    quadrant-3 Tutorial\n    quadrant-4 \"How-to guide\"\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is the canonical Diátaxis grid; see \u003ca href=\"https://diataxis.fr/\" class=\"okf-external\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ehttps://diataxis.fr/\u003c/a\u003e for the full treatment.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"how-this-bundle-maps-the-four-types\"\u003eHow this bundle maps the four types\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis bundle adopts Diátaxis by making the framework's four content types the four subdirectories of the bundle — and, crucially, by using each type as the OKF \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e frontmatter value of the concepts inside it. The Diátaxis type and the OKF type are the same field.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eDiátaxis type\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eThis bundle's directory\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eOKF \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e value\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eTutorial\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etutorials/\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etype: Tutorial\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eHow-to guide\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003ehow-to/\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etype: How-to\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eReference\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003ereference/\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etype: Reference\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eExplanation\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003eexplanation/\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etype: Explanation\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eEach directory has an \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e that lists its concepts, and the bundle's root \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e frames the four quadrants for a reader arriving at the top. A reader who lands on any concept can read its \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e and immediately know what posture the page is written for.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is more than a filing scheme. The \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e value is a \u003cstrong\u003epromise\u003c/strong\u003e the author makes about the page's shape:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eA \u003ccode\u003eTutorial\u003c/code\u003e \u003cem\u003ewill\u003c/em\u003e walk a beginner through runnable steps. If it assumes prior knowledge, it is miscategorised.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eA \u003ccode\u003eHow-to\u003c/code\u003e \u003cem\u003ewill\u003c/em\u003e solve one real-world goal and assume the basics. If it stops to teach, it has drifted into Tutorial.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eA \u003ccode\u003eReference\u003c/code\u003e \u003cem\u003ewill\u003c/em\u003e describe the machinery neutrally. If it argues a design choice, that argument belongs in Explanation; if it gives steps, those belong in How-to.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAn \u003ccode\u003eExplanation\u003c/code\u003e \u003cem\u003ewill\u003c/em\u003e discuss the why and compare alternatives. If it starts listing steps, those belong in How-to.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-mixing-the-types-confuses-readers\"\u003eWhy mixing the types confuses readers\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe reason the framework is strict about separation is that the postures are mutually exclusive in the moment. A reader in the middle of a task (How-to posture) is not also learning the basics (Tutorial posture); a reader looking up a flag (Reference posture) is not also absorbing a design argument (Explanation posture). When a single page tries to serve two postures, it serves both badly.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eConsider a \u003ccode\u003evalidate\u003c/code\u003e command page. The Reference version is a table of flags and exit codes. The How-to version is \"Validate a bundle in CI\" — a recipe that picks the right flags for a CI pipeline. The Explanation version is \"Why there are three validation profiles\" — an argument about audiences. All three are about \u003ccode\u003evalidate\u003c/code\u003e; none of them should be the same document. A reader who wants the flag table does not want the argument; a reader who wants the argument does not want the recipe; a reader who wants the recipe does not want either.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis bundle enforces the split structurally. The same \u003ccode\u003evalidate\u003c/code\u003e command appears in:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/how-to/validate_in_ci.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eValidate a bundle in CI\u003c/a\u003e — the recipe.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/reference/cli.md#validate\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eCLI command reference\u003c/a\u003e — the neutral flag table.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e(And the design choice behind the profiles is argued here, in an Explanation, when relevant.)\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree postures, three pages, one topic. The reader picks the page that matches their posture.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003eDiátaxis's own guidance is blunt on this point: a document that mixes types is not a stronger document — it is a weaker one, because it\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp\u003efails every reader it tries to serve simultaneously.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-diátaxis-maps-so-cleanly-onto-okf\"\u003eWhy Diátaxis maps so cleanly onto OKF\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe reason this bundle can adopt Diátaxis without a format change is that OKF already declines to impose a type taxonomy (SPEC §1 non-goal) while listing example \u003ccode\u003etype\u003c/code\u003e values (\u003ccode\u003eBigQuery Table\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ePlaybook\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eReference\u003c/code\u003e, …). A documentation bundle that wants Diátaxis simply \u003cem\u003euses\u003c/em\u003e the four type names as its \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e values; the format treats them like any other producer-defined string and okf-loom preserves them round-trip.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is the SPEC §2 round-trip rule in action: producers may add any keys; consumers must preserve them. Diátaxis is not a special case to okf-loom — it is one of many possible type vocabularies a bundle can adopt. A data-catalog bundle would use domain types (\u003ccode\u003eBigQuery Table\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eDataset\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eMetric\u003c/code\u003e); a playbooks bundle would use \u003ccode\u003ePlaybook\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003eRunbook\u003c/code\u003e; this documentation bundle uses the four Diátaxis types. None of them requires a spec change or a capability declaration, because \u003ccode\u003etype\u003c/code\u003e is a free-form string and okf-loom auto-colours the graph by type hash regardless of vocabulary.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe capability registry even has a \u003ccode\u003eokf.cap.diataxis_types\u003c/code\u003e capability for bundles that want okf-loom to \u003cem\u003erecognise\u003c/em\u003e the four types and validate their conventional sections (tutorials have steps; reference has schema; explanation has no steps). That capability is recognised-if-present and never required — consistent with okf-loom's posture that type vocabularies are a bundle's choice, not a spec mandate. See \u003ca href=\"/reference/capabilities.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003ecapabilities.md\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"how-to-read-this-bundle\"\u003eHow to read this bundle\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWith the framework in mind, the bundle's shape is self-explaining:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNew to okf-loom?\u003c/strong\u003e Start in \u003ca href=\"/tutorials/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eTutorials\u003c/a\u003e and read top to bottom, reproducing each step.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHave a specific task?\u003c/strong\u003e Jump to \u003ca href=\"/how-to/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eHow-to guides\u003c/a\u003e and find the recipe.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLooking up a fact?\u003c/strong\u003e Open \u003ca href=\"/reference/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eReference\u003c/a\u003e and find the page.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWant the why?\u003c/strong\u003e Read \u003ca href=\"/explanation/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eExplanation\u003c/a\u003e — you are in it right now.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe four postures are also cross-linked. A tutorial that uses the CLI links to the CLI reference; a reference page links to the how-to that exercises it; an explanation links to both the tutorial where the choice manifests and the reference that describes the machinery. The links are what let a reader change posture without losing their place.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"when-diátaxis-is-the-wrong-choice\"\u003eWhen Diátaxis is the wrong choice\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis bundle is documentation, so Diátaxis fits. The framework is explicitly a \u003cem\u003edocumentation\u003c/em\u003e taxonomy, not a domain taxonomy, and it does not fit every bundle. A data catalog's types are domain-specific (\u003ccode\u003eBigQuery Table\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eAPI Endpoint\u003c/code\u003e); a playbooks bundle's types are operational (\u003ccode\u003eRunbook\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ePlaybook\u003c/code\u003e); a knowledge graph's types are the entities themselves. Forcing Diátaxis onto those bundles would be a category error — it would impose a documentation vocabulary on content that is not documentation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eokf-loom's stance, reflected in \u003ca href=\"/explanation/research.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/explanation/research.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e §13, is that Diátaxis is a \u003cem\u003estrong recommended default for doc-oriented bundles\u003c/em\u003e and \u003cem\u003eirrelevant for domain catalogs\u003c/em\u003e. This bundle is a doc-oriented bundle, so it adopts the framework. A bundle that is not should pick the type vocabulary that matches its domain — the format and okf-loom support both equally.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"see-also\"\u003eSee also\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/tutorials/first_bundle.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eAuthor your first bundle\u003c/a\u003e — where the Tutorial posture shows up in practice.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/how-to/validate_in_ci.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eValidate a bundle in CI\u003c/a\u003e — a How-to guide in its pure form.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/reference/cli.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eCLI command reference\u003c/a\u003e — the Reference posture.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/reference/frontmatter.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eFrontmatter contract\u003c/a\u003e — the \u003ccode\u003etype:\u003c/code\u003e key this framework uses as its vocabulary.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/reference/capabilities.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eCapability registry\u003c/a\u003e — the \u003ccode\u003eokf.cap.diataxis_types\u003c/code\u003e capability, recognised-if-present.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://diataxis.fr/\" class=\"okf-external\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eDiátaxis\u003c/a\u003e — the source framework.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"/explanation/research.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e/explanation/research.md\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e §13 — the comparative note that framed Diátaxis as an optional type taxonomy.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eReturn to \u003ca href=\"/explanation/index.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eExplanation\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e", "explanation/live_studio_design": "\u003ch2 id=\"why-the-live-studio-exists\"\u003eWhy the live studio exists\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis essay explains the reasoning behind the live collaborative studio. It is not the tutorial for using the studio — that is \u003ca href=\"/tutorials/live_studio_basics.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eUse the live studio\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"/tutorials/author_with_agent.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eDirect the agent loop\u003c/a\u003e — and it is not the neutral reference for its routes and state model — that is \u003ca href=\"/reference/http_routes.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eHTTP server routes\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"/reference/comment_lifecycle.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eComment lifecycle and archive rules\u003c/a\u003e. It is the \u003cem\u003ewhy\u003c/em\u003e behind those surfaces.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe binding design document is the \u003ca href=\"/reference/spec.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003ecurrent okf-loom spec\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e; this essay summarises its live-studio posture (§10) and decisions at a readable length and links out for depth.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-posture-the-studio-is-built-on\"\u003eThe posture the studio is built on\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe studio rests on a single founding claim, stated as decision \u003cstrong\u003eD8\u003c/strong\u003e and design posture §1.1 of the spec:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe agent is the author and the manager of the OKF files. Writing OKF files \u003cem\u003eis\u003c/em\u003e the agent's job.\u003c/strong\u003e Its mechanical \u003cem\u003eand\u003c/em\u003e semantic edits apply directly through the mutators; they appear live and land in the change list with one-click undo. The user's safety net is \u003cstrong\u003etransparency plus undo\u003c/strong\u003e, not an approval step.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eEverything else in the studio follows from that. If the agent is the author, then the user does not need an editor — they need a \u003cem\u003edirecting\u003c/em\u003e surface. If the agent edits freely, then the safety net has to be \u003cem\u003esee-and-undo\u003c/em\u003e, not \u003cem\u003ereview-before-write\u003c/em\u003e. If the user is the sole admin, then nothing should gate them, and the only protections that remain are the ones that defend against things that are \u003cem\u003enot\u003c/em\u003e the user.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-comment-driven-directing\"\u003eWhy comment-driven directing\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe studio's primary user interaction is a \u003cstrong\u003ecomment\u003c/strong\u003e — a short directive the user attaches to a concept, a section, a text selection, or a frontmatter key. The user does not hand-edit markdown in the browser; they point and comment, and the agent authors the files.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eThe alternative considered\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eWhy the studio chose comments instead\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA direct in-browser markdown editor\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eIntroduces a user↔agent merge problem (concurrent edits to the same file), requires CRDT/OT, and still needs a separate channel to \u003cem\u003etell\u003c/em\u003e the agent what to do. The agent is the sole writer of \u003ccode\u003e.md\u003c/code\u003e files, so there is no merge problem to solve day-to-day.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA chat sidebar that dispatches commands\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eCollapses \"where is this about\" into \"what is this about\". A comment anchored to a schema row carries both: it names the target \u003cem\u003eand\u003c/em\u003e the intent.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA queue of typed actions (button per verb)\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eForecloses the open-ended asks (\"rewrite this section from the spec\", \"extract these columns into their own concepts\") that are the actual daily work. Free-text comments with an anchor cover all of them.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA comment is the steering wheel; the change list plus undo (§12.2 / §12.5 of the spec) is the review surface. The user reads in Rendered / Source / Split — all read-only — and directs; the agent claims a comment, does its scoped work, writes via the ordinary mutators, and resolves it, linking the activity entries it produced. The canonical loop is documented in \u003ca href=\"/tutorials/author_with_agent.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eDirect the agent loop\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe user can still edit files directly on disk in their own editor — that is their machine, and the watcher picks it up. The studio web UI is a \u003cem\u003edirecting\u003c/em\u003e surface, not a direct editor.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-there-is-no-review-gate-by-default\"\u003eWhy there is no review gate by default\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is the most often-questioned choice, so it is worth being precise.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA review gate is the idea that the agent proposes edits and a human approves each one before it lands. The studio ships \u003cem\u003ewithout\u003c/em\u003e one, and the reasoning is that a review gate optimises for the wrong failure mode. The daily failure mode of an agent authoring a knowledge bundle is not \"the agent wrote something malicious and we stopped it\" — the agent is the user's own, running locally, on the user's own files. The daily failure mode is \"the agent wrote the wrong \u003cem\u003egood\u003c/em\u003e edit, and the user wants to revert it in one click.\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThat argues for a fast, visible \u003cstrong\u003eundo\u003c/strong\u003e, not a slow, gating \u003cstrong\u003eapprove\u003c/strong\u003e. So the studio invests in three things instead of a gate:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eA live change list\u003c/strong\u003e — a read-only timeline of everything that happened, with actor, action, affected concepts, and a timestamp.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePer-write undo snapshots\u003c/strong\u003e — prior bytes captured before every agent write under \u003ccode\u003e.okf-loom/session/history/\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eGroup undo\u003c/strong\u003e — a single agent pass that writes several files is recorded as one group (a shared \u003ccode\u003egroup_id\u003c/code\u003e), so the user reverts the whole pass with one click, not file-by-file.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA user who genuinely \u003cem\u003ewants\u003c/em\u003e to restrain their own agent — propose-only mode, forbidden paths, per-action caps — can opt in via \u003ccode\u003estudio.constraints\u003c/code\u003e (spec §12.3). The studio ships the \u003cem\u003eseam\u003c/em\u003e (the \u003ccode\u003e/__apply\u003c/code\u003e endpoint and the \u003ccode\u003eproposals.jsonl\u003c/code\u003e contract) but never the \u003cem\u003epolicy\u003c/em\u003e. That keeps the default experience frictionless and lets a user build whatever restraint they want as their own module.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-everything-is-on-by-default\"\u003eWhy everything is on by default\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom serve \u0026lt;bundle\u0026gt;\u003c/code\u003e — with no flags — opens the full studio: live SSE updates, source and split views, commenting, directing, agent presence, the change list, and undo. There is no \u003ccode\u003e--edit\u003c/code\u003e to unlock, no per-save consent, and no permission prompt.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe reasoning is that the studio's value is \u003cem\u003ecollaboration that feels alive\u003c/em\u003e, and collaboration you have to assemble out of flags is collaboration that does not happen. Every default that is off by default is a feature the user has to discover, and the studio's P0 bar (spec §1.7) is judged on how alive it feels out of the box, not on how many features it has behind toggles.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe defaults that remain are the ones that cost the user \u003cem\u003ezero friction\u003c/em\u003e and defend against things that are not the user (see the trust model below). Editing, saving, and watching are never behind a gate; only the loopback boundary, the cross-origin guard, and the active-code gate are — and the first two are invisible to a local user.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-server-sent-events-with-a-polling-fallback\"\u003eWhy Server-Sent Events, with a polling fallback\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eLive push is Server-Sent Events (SSE) over plain HTTP, served from the stdlib \u003ccode\u003eThreadingHTTPServer\u003c/code\u003e. The spec records this as decision \u003cstrong\u003eD0\u003c/strong\u003e: SSE plus REST, not WebSocket.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eThe alternative considered\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eWhy SSE won\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWebSocket\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eRicher bidirectional channel, but the studio's traffic is asymmetric (server pushes change/presence/comment events; client sends occasional POSTs). WebSocket would add a dependency surface and a protocol layer for a need SSE already meets with one worker thread per stream under stdlib.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePure polling\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eSimpler, but a polling interval short enough to feel live burns cycles doing nothing, and an interval long enough to be cheap feels sluggish. SSE pushes the moment a change lands.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe one real-world failure of raw SSE is that some intermediaries — Cloudflare quick tunnels, corporate proxies, certain CDNs — buffer the \u003ccode\u003etext/event-stream\u003c/code\u003e response, so \u003ccode\u003eEventSource\u003c/code\u003e connects but never receives frames. The studio handles this with a \u003cstrong\u003estarvation watchdog\u003c/strong\u003e: if no SSE frame arrives within a grace window (~5s), the client arms a polling fallback that fetches \u003ccode\u003e/__data/events?since=…\u003c/code\u003e on a short interval and dispatches through the \u003cem\u003esame\u003c/em\u003e handler path as SSE. If SSE recovers, the poller stops. The no-refresh contract therefore survives behind a proxy that would silently starve SSE alone (spec §7.3).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis matters because the no-refresh contract is a P0 requirement, not polish: a full-page reload after every agent edit would discard the user's scroll position, selection, view mode, and open comment threads. The studio patches the smallest affected region and preserves all of that state (spec §7.3).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-archive-is-a-separate-track\"\u003eWhy archive is a separate track\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA comment carries two independent pieces of state:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eTrack\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eField\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eValues\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eMeaning\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eLifecycle\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003estate\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003eopen\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eclaimed\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003eresolved\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003edismissed\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eWhere the work is.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003eVisibility\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003earchived\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etrue\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003efalse\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eWhether the panel soft-hides the thread.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eArchiving a resolved comment keeps it resolved; unarchiving restores the prior visibility without flipping \u003ccode\u003estate\u003c/code\u003e. Compatibility records with \u003ccode\u003estate == \"archived\"\u003c/code\u003e are normalised on read to \u003ccode\u003earchived=true, state=\"open\"\u003c/code\u003e so old sessions migrate automatically.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe archive track also carries three server-side rules that make it behave predictably:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eArchive is root-only.\u003c/strong\u003e Replies cannot be archived independently; the whole thread archives together.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eArchive is gated on whole-thread-resolved.\u003c/strong\u003e The server returns \u003ccode\u003e409\u003c/code\u003e with the unresolved ids if any comment in the thread is not yet \u003ccode\u003eresolved\u003c/code\u003e, so the user cannot accidentally hide unfinished work.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eReplying to an archived thread auto-unarchives the parent.\u003c/strong\u003e Adding to a thread reopens it for business; archive is a soft hide, not a closed state.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe full state model is in \u003ca href=\"/reference/comment_lifecycle.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eComment lifecycle and archive rules\u003c/a\u003e; the step-by-step recipe is in \u003ca href=\"/how-to/archive_threads.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eArchive and resolve comment threads\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-trust-model-gate-the-port-and-the-code-not-the-person\"\u003eThe trust model: gate the port and the code, not the person\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe studio is single-user local-admin. There is exactly one human, and they own everything — the bundle \u003cem\u003eand\u003c/em\u003e the agent that works for them. The studio \u003cstrong\u003enever gates, prompts, or flag-guards the user\u003c/strong\u003e. What it keeps are the protections that defend against things that are \u003cem\u003enot\u003c/em\u003e the user, and the spec is explicit (§15) that these must cost the user zero friction.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable class=\"okf-table\"\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003cth\u003eProtection\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eWhat it stops\u003c/th\u003e\u003cth\u003eWhat it does NOT stop\u003c/th\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLoopback by default\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e127.0.0.1\u003c/code\u003e)\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eOther machines reaching the studio. Exposing the port is an explicit \u003ccode\u003e--public\u003c/code\u003e plus an acknowledgement.\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eThe user or their agent.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePer-session CSRF token\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003eX-OKF-Token\u003c/code\u003e, written \u003ccode\u003e0600\u003c/code\u003e)\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA random web page POSTing to the localhost studio behind the user's back.\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eThe studio's own page, which carries the token automatically.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOrigin AND Host allow-list\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eCross-site and DNS-rebinding attacks (checking both closes a hole that forging only \u003ccode\u003eOrigin\u003c/code\u003e could exploit).\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eThe user's own requests from an allowed host.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTwo-layer active-code gate\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eA \u003cem\u003edownloaded bundle\u003c/em\u003e trying to run code (JS / full-HTML overrides / viewer plugins) in the user's browser.\u003c/td\u003e\u003ctd\u003eEditing, saving, and watching — those are explicitly not behind this gate.\u003c/td\u003e\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe summary the spec arrives at — and that this essay will end on — is:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWe gate the port and the bundle's code, never the user or their agent.\u003c/strong\u003e The user's safety net for agent-authored edits is the live change list plus (group) undo, not an approval step.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eData-safety invariants (validate-before-write, path containment, atomic writes, optimistic per-doc \u003ccode\u003erev\u003c/code\u003e) are kept too, but they are framed as \u003cem\u003ecorrectness\u003c/em\u003e guards, not \u003cem\u003epermission\u003c/em\u003e guards: they stop corruption and lost work, not access. The single collision case the studio has to handle — the user editing a file directly on disk at the same moment the agent writes it — surfaces non-destructively as a \u003ccode\u003e409\u003c/code\u003e with a diff, never as a silent clobber (spec §9.3 / §9.4).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"why-the-server-stays-llm-free\"\u003eWhy the server stays LLM-free\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA final choice worth naming is that \u003cstrong\u003ethe server never runs the agent.\u003c/strong\u003e The server emits events, runs mechanical operations (index regen, relation mirroring), and serves the studio; all semantic work is done by the external agent (opencode / Claude Code / Codex / a custom harness), which watches the change feed, reacts to comments, reasons, and writes back through the ordinary mutators.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe reasons are the current non-goals: the checkout runtime stays harness-agnostic (no opinion on which agent framework consumes it), keeps the primary runtime dependency-light (no model bundled, no GPU assumed, no network required), and keeps the collaboration working headlessly (\u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom watch\u003c/code\u003e tails the same change feed with no browser at all). The agent loop — \u003ccode\u003escripts/okf-loom wait\u003c/code\u003e blocks in the foreground, the agent claims, writes via mutators, resolves — is the same shape whether the studio is open or not. See \u003ca href=\"/tutorials/author_with_agent.md\" class=\"okf-internal\"\u003eDirect the agent loop\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"see-also\"\u003eSee See \u003ccode\u003escripts/okf_loom/viewer/OVERRIDES.md\u003c/code\u003e §5 and current spec §15.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003ch4 id=\"chosen-by-us\"\u003eChosen by us\u003c/h4\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eGLiNER NER + LLM discovery (capability stubs ship; no ML dependency in core).\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"change-control\"\u003eChange control\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eIf scope changes after the v1.0 baseline:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\u003cli\u003eAdd the new requirement as a row in the matrix above.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eBump \u003ccode\u003eLOOM_VERSION\u003c/code\u003e in \u003ccode\u003escripts/okf_loom/__init__.py\u003c/code\u003e and update the current spec plus any publication notes used for the next release.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAdd tests under \u003ccode\u003etests/\u003c/code\u003e that pin the new behaviour.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eUpdate \u003ccode\u003eSKILL.md\u003c/code\u003e and the relevant focused resource under \u003ccode\u003eresources/\u003c/code\u003e if the user-facing surface changes.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e", "explanation/research": "\u003ch2 id=\"okf-loom-best-of-breed-research\"\u003eokf-loom — Best-of-Breed Research\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNote:\u003c/strong\u003e this document is retained research input for the v1.0 baseline. Several recommendations it makes — a local dense-embedding backend (\u003ccode\u003esentence-transformers\u003c/code\u003e), a \u003ccode\u003e[semantic]\u003c/code\u003e extra, an \u003ccode\u003e[llm]\u003c/code\u003e extra, a portable \u003ccode\u003evectors.jsonl\u003c/code\u003e reader, and an on-disk SQLite FTS table — were prototyped and \u003cstrong\u003elater removed\u003c/strong\u003e. The surviving search story is fully zero-dependency: lexical (BM25) + fuzzy-semantic (\u003ccode\u003eSemanticLite\u003c/code\u003e)\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003ehybrid (RRF fusion). The reasoning: the agent (an LLM in opencode /\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eClaude Code / Codex) is itself the best true-semantic engine, so a local embedding backend is redundant; \u003ccode\u003eSemanticLite\u003c/code\u003e stays as a cheap fuzzy-semantic layer that helps the agent find candidates. Read the dense/\u003ccode\u003e[semantic]\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003e[llm]\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003evector-index\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003esqlite-fts\u003c/code\u003e passages below as \"explored, then dropped,\" not as the current runtime surface. The current surface lives in \u003ccode\u003eSKILL.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eresources/advanced-operations.md\u003c/code\u003e, and \u003ccode\u003edocs-bundle/reference/architecture.md\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eStatus:\u003c/strong\u003e Research input for the architect and implementation subagents. \u003cstrong\u003eScope:\u003c/strong\u003e What okf-loom (validator, structure/link/content checks, wiki viewer, lexical + semantic search, auto-discovery, plugin extension points) should borrow from existing knowledge/documentation tools. \u003cstrong\u003eMethod:\u003c/strong\u003e Facts gathered from upstream READMEs/docs (Quartz, MkDocs Material, Dendron, sentence-transformers, sqlite-vec, LanceDB, GLiNER, MiniSearch, Lunr, Pagefind, the OKF SPEC v0.1) plus established, stable behavior of the commercial/hosted systems. \u003cstrong\u003eGrounding note (important):\u003c/strong\u003e The task brief references an \"upstream OKF \u003ccode\u003eviz.html\u003c/code\u003e\" that embeds the bundle as JSON with Cytoscape.js + marked. As of the current upstream \u003ccode\u003eGoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog\u003c/code\u003e \u003ccode\u003eokf/\u003c/code\u003e tree (SPEC v0.1 — Draft), \u003cstrong\u003eno \u003ccode\u003eviz.html\u003c/code\u003e exists\u003c/strong\u003e; the tree is \u003ccode\u003eSPEC.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ebundles/\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003esamples/\u003c/code\u003e (\u003ccode\u003ecrypto_bitcoin\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ega4_merch_store\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003estackoverflow\u003c/code\u003e), \u003ccode\u003esrc/\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003etests/\u003c/code\u003e. This document therefore treats the described Cytoscape+marked, single-self-contained-HTML pattern as a \u003cem\u003ereference design to evaluate\u003c/em\u003e, not an existing artifact, and Section 15 compares it on those merits.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eOKF essentials assumed throughout (per SPEC §3–§11): bundle = directory tree; concept = YAML frontmatter (\u003ccode\u003etype\u003c/code\u003e required; \u003ccode\u003etitle\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003edescription\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eresource\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003etags\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003etimestamp\u003c/code\u003e recommended; arbitrary keys allowed); reserved \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e (progressive-disclosure listing) and \u003ccode\u003elog.md\u003c/code\u003e (ISO-8601 \u003ccode\u003eYYYY-MM-DD\u003c/code\u003e dated history, newest first); concept ID = path sans \u003ccode\u003e.md\u003c/code\u003e; cross-links absolute (\u003ccode\u003e/tables/users.md\u003c/code\u003e, RECOMMENDED) or relative (\u003ccode\u003e./other.md\u003c/code\u003e); consumers MUST tolerate broken links; conventional body headings \u003ccode\u003e# Schema\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003e# Examples\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003e# Citations\u003c/code\u003e; bundles MAY declare \u003ccode\u003eokf_version\u003c/code\u003e in a root \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e; minor = additive, major = breaking.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSystems are ordered by \u003cstrong\u003erelevance to OKF\u003c/strong\u003e, not alphabetically.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"1-quartz-v4-highest-relevance-published-obsidian-style-vaults\"\u003e1. Quartz v4  \u003cem\u003e(highest relevance — published Obsidian-style vaults)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(a) What it is.\u003c/strong\u003e Quartz is a static-site generator that turns a folder of interlinked markdown (\"digital garden\") into a website. It is the closest existing analog to the OKF viewer, and it is explicitly built around the same primitives OKF standardizes: markdown + YAML frontmatter, \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e overrides, tag/folder listing pages, cross-links, broken-link tolerance.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(b) Mechanisms worth stealing.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePlugin pipeline = map / filter / reduce over content.\u003c/strong\u003e This is the single most transferable idea. Quartz config (\u003ccode\u003equartz.config.ts\u003c/code\u003e) declares \u003ccode\u003etransformers\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003efilters\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eemitters\u003c/code\u003e:\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eTransformers\u003c/em\u003e \u003cstrong\u003emap\u003c/strong\u003e over each content node, in order (e.g. \u003ccode\u003eFrontMatter\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eCreatedModifiedDate\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eSyntaxHighlighting\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eObsidianFlavoredMarkdown\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eGitHubFlavoredMarkdown\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eTableOfContents\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eCrawlLinks\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eDescription\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eLatex\u003c/code\u003e). Some are position-sensitive.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eFilters\u003c/em\u003e \u003cstrong\u003edecide\u003c/strong\u003e which nodes emit (e.g. \u003ccode\u003eRemoveDrafts\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eEmitters\u003c/em\u003e \u003cstrong\u003ereduce\u003c/strong\u003e across the whole set (e.g. \u003ccode\u003eFolderPage\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eTagPage\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eContentIndex\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eAssets\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eStatic\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eRSS\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eAliasRedirects\u003c/code\u003e). This is a clean, ordered, composable pipeline — an almost exact fit for OKF's \"validator / structure checks / link checks / content checks / index+log generation / viewer build\" stages. OKF should adopt this three-phase taxonomy directly.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOne shared content index feeds many features.\u003c/strong\u003e The \u003ccode\u003eContentIndex\u003c/code\u003e emitter produces a single \u003ccode\u003econtentIndex.json\u003c/code\u003e that \u003cstrong\u003eboth full-text search and the graph view consume\u003c/strong\u003e. Don't build separate indexes per feature; emit one canonical graph+document model and let components read it. (SPEC §4.2 already nudges toward \"structural markdown\" — the index should preserve headings/lists/tables, not just flat text.)\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLink resolution as a first-class, configurable transformer.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eCrawlLinks\u003c/code\u003e exposes \u003ccode\u003emarkdownLinkResolution: \"absolute\" | \"relative\" | \"shortest\"\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003eprettyLinks\u003c/code\u003e (strip folder paths in display text). OKF's link rules (SPEC §5: absolute RECOMMENDED, relative allowed, broken links tolerated) map 1:1 onto this; the validator should implement the same resolution modes and the viewer should rewrite links for whatever serving context it's in.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFrontmatter parsing with alias collapsing.\u003c/strong\u003e Quartz's \u003ccode\u003eFrontmatter\u003c/code\u003e transformer (built on \u003ccode\u003egray-matter\u003c/code\u003e) accepts YAML or TOML, configurable delimiters, and \u003cstrong\u003ecollapses many source aliases to canonical fields\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003etags\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003etag\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ealiases\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003ealias\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ecreated\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003edate\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003emodified\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003elastmod\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eupdated\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003elast-modified\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003edraft\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003epublish\u003c/code\u003e). OKF should do the same: a small alias map per canonical field, so producer variety doesn't break consumption (and aligns with SPEC §9's \"preserve unknown keys, tolerate variety\").\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAuto-generated folder/tag listings that hand-authored files override.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eFolderPage\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003eTagPage\u003c/code\u003e emitters synthesize listing pages, but if a directory already contains a hand-written \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e (with \u003ccode\u003etitle\u003c/code\u003e), Quartz uses \u003cem\u003ethat\u003c/em\u003e instead. Tag hierarchies (\u003ccode\u003eplugin/emitter\u003c/code\u003e) render one page per tag level plus a global \u003ccode\u003e/tags\u003c/code\u003e index. This is exactly the OKF §6 model and gives a clean answer to \"regenerate \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e without destroying hand-curated content\" (Section C): \u003cstrong\u003esynthesize by default, defer to any existing hand-authored file, and only touch generated regions.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eGraph view.\u003c/strong\u003e Local graph (all notes ≤1 hop away) + global graph; node radius ∝ degree; visited nodes colored differently; force-directed with tunable \u003ccode\u003erepelForce\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003ecenterForce\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003elinkDistance\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003edepth\u003c/code\u003e; an Obsidian-style radial mode. Runs client-side off \u003ccode\u003econtentIndex.json\u003c/code\u003e. Cheap and high-impact.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFull-text search.\u003c/strong\u003e Powered by \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/nextapps-de/flexsearch\" class=\"okf-external\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eFlexSearch\u003c/a\u003e; \"\u0026lt;10ms for half a million words.\" Strips markdown syntax before indexing, builds \u003cstrong\u003eseparate indexes for title/content/tags with title weighted highest\u003c/strong\u003e, tokenizes CJK, exposes tag search via a \u003ccode\u003e#\u003c/code\u003e-prefix or \u003ccode\u003eCtrl+Shift+K\u003c/code\u003e. Fully keyboard-navigable.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOther portable patterns:\u003c/strong\u003e SPA routing (relative URLs so it works \"no matter where you deploy\"); \u003ccode\u003eignorePatterns\u003c/code\u003e (globs for private/templates); \u003ccode\u003eenablePopovers\u003c/code\u003e (Wikipedia-style hover preview using a \u003ccode\u003epopover-hint\u003c/code\u003e CSS class to select what to preview); composable layout via \u003ccode\u003eFlex\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eMobileOnly\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eDesktopOnly\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eConditionalRender\u003c/code\u003e; a philosophy of \u003cstrong\u003ethree customization tiers\u003c/strong\u003e (content-only / config knobs / full source) — directly applicable to \"embeddable in any agent/meta-harness.\"\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(c) What does NOT translate.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eQuartz is \u003cstrong\u003eTypeScript/Node\u003c/strong\u003e, opinionated for \u003cem\u003epublishing personal gardens\u003c/em\u003e. OKF is Python-first, harness-agnostic, and must validate/transform as a library, not just render a site. Steal the \u003cem\u003epipeline architecture\u003c/em\u003e, not the toolchain.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eQuartz's wikilink/transclusion syntax (\u003ccode\u003e![[...]]\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003e[[x#^block]]\u003c/code\u003e) is richer than OKF's standard-markdown links. OKF should support only standard markdown links + its two resolution modes, and treat wikilinks as an \u003cem\u003eopt-in transformer\u003c/em\u003e (the \u003ccode\u003eObsidianFlavoredMarkdown\u003c/code\u003e plugin), never core.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003ebaseUrl\u003c/code\u003e/analytics/CDN-font concerns are publishing concerns, not knowledge-format concerns.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat OKF should steal:\u003c/strong\u003e the \u003cstrong\u003etransformer / filter / emitter pipeline\u003c/strong\u003e as the core extension model; a \u003cstrong\u003esingle canonical content index\u003c/strong\u003e (graph + docs) consumed by search, graph view, and listings; \u003cstrong\u003econfigurable link resolution\u003c/strong\u003e (absolute/relative/shortest) + \u003cstrong\u003efrontmatter alias collapsing\u003c/strong\u003e; \u003cstrong\u003esynthesize-but-don't-clobber\u003c/strong\u003e behavior for \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e/tag pages; \u003cstrong\u003elocal + global graph\u003c/strong\u003e with degree-weighted nodes; \u003cstrong\u003efield-weighted, markdown-stripped full-text search\u003c/strong\u003e with tag-mode; the \u003cstrong\u003ethree-tier customization philosophy\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"2-obsidian-the-reference-ux-consumers-expect\"\u003e2. Obsidian  \u003cem\u003e(the reference UX consumers expect)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(a) What it is.\u003c/strong\u003e A local-first personal knowledge base: a \"vault\" = a folder of markdown. Closed-source desktop/mobile app with a deep plugin ecosystem. It is the de-facto UX benchmark; OKF's viewer will be judged against it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(b) Mechanisms worth stealing.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBacklinks panel + outgoing links panel + unlinked mentions.\u003c/strong\u003e Obsidian shows, per note, what links \u003cem\u003eto\u003c/em\u003e it, what it links \u003cem\u003eto\u003c/em\u003e, and \u003cem\u003eplain-text mentions of the note's title that aren't yet links\u003c/em\u003e (\"unlinked mentions\" with a one-click convert-to-link). The last one is \u003cstrong\u003edirectly an auto-discovery primitive\u003c/strong\u003e: OKF's \"discover missing links\" can mine unlinked mentions of known concept titles/IDs across bodies. High leverage.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eGraph view\u003c/strong\u003e (force-directed, filterable by tag/path/search, color by folder/tag/created-time, drag/zoom). Same idea as Quartz, richer filters.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTags + nested tags\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e#area/data\u003c/code\u003e, navigable). SPEC §4.1 makes tags first-class; nested tags are a cheap win for browsing.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWikilinks \u003ccode\u003e[[note]]\u003c/code\u003e vs markdown links\u003c/strong\u003e with a \u003cem\u003econfigurable default\u003c/em\u003e and graceful coexistence. OKF keeps standard markdown links as canonical, but should \u003cem\u003eaccept\u003c/em\u003e wikilinks as a soft input.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTransclusion/embeds\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e![[note]]\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003e![[](image.png|100x100)]]\u003c/code\u003e). For OKF, an optional \"embed concept\" transformer that inlines another concept's \u003ccode\u003e# Schema\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003e# Examples\u003c/code\u003e section at render time — useful, but keep it as a plugin.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDataview plugin\u003c/strong\u003e (query your vault with a SQL-like/JS DSL over frontmatter + the link graph, render as tables/lists). This is the \"relations/queries\" primitive OKF should offer over its content index (see Notion §4 and Synthesis A).\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePlugin architecture\u003c/strong\u003e (manifest + lifecycle hooks + settings tab; community plugins via a registry). Inspires OKF's plugin contract.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(c) What does NOT translate.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eProprietary binary cache\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e.obsidian/\u003c/code\u003e) and a desktop GUI. OKF is plain files + a server/static HTML.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBlock references\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e^id\u003c/code\u003e) require stable, author-maintained anchors — heavy for a generator-written format; OKF should link to \u003cem\u003econcepts\u003c/em\u003e and \u003cem\u003eheadings\u003c/em\u003e, not arbitrary blocks.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWikilink-as-default\u003c/strong\u003e conflicts with SPEC §5's standard-markdown + absolute-path recommendation. Wikilinks are a convenience layer only.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat OKF should steal:\u003c/strong\u003e \u003cstrong\u003eunlinked-mentions → link suggestions\u003c/strong\u003e (core discovery); backlinks/outgoing panels; \u003cstrong\u003eDataview-style queries\u003c/strong\u003e over the content index as a first-class feature; nested tags; an optional transclusion transformer; the \u003cem\u003efeel\u003c/em\u003e of a plugin registry.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"3-mkdocs-material-reference-for-docs-site-conventions\"\u003e3. MkDocs Material  \u003cem\u003e(reference for docs-site conventions)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(a) What it is.\u003c/strong\u003e The most popular MkDocs theme: markdown → polished, searchable static docs site. Server-rendered (Python \u003ccode\u003emkdocs build\u003c/code\u003e), statically hostable anywhere.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(b) Mechanisms worth stealing.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003enav\u003c/code\u003e + auto-discovery.\u003c/strong\u003e Explicit \u003ccode\u003enav\u003c/code\u003e in \u003ccode\u003emkdocs.yml\u003c/code\u003e for hand-curated order, with auto-discovery fallback. Maps to OKF's hand-authored \u003ccode\u003eindex.md\u003c/code\u003e vs synthesized listings (Quartz §1 pattern again).\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBuilt-in \u003ccode\u003etags\u003c/code\u003e plugin\u003c/strong\u003e (tags index, tag listings, \u003ccode\u003etags.yml\u003c/code\u003e metadata) — the same \"synthesize tag pages\" idea, mature and well-tested.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBuilt-in \u003ccode\u003esearch\u003c/code\u003e plugin\u003c/strong\u003e (lexicographic, section-aware, highlighting) and optional \u003cstrong\u003eAlgolia DocSearch\u003c/strong\u003e integration for large corpora. The \"small built-in + optional hosted backend\" split is exactly OKF's \"zero-dep baseline + pluggable semantic backend.\"\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eblog\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003eprojects\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e plugins (chronological posts; monorepo of sub-docs). The blog model maps to OKF's \u003ccode\u003elog.md\u003c/code\u003e (date-grouped, newest-first) — a viewer could render \u003ccode\u003elog.md\u003c/code\u003e as a timeline.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHooks\u003c/strong\u003e (Python event functions: \u003ccode\u003eon_page_markdown\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eon_page_content\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eon_config\u003c/code\u003e, …) — the canonical \u003cem\u003eserver-side\u003c/em\u003e plugin contract; pairs naturally with OKF's Python base.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSnippet includes\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e--8\u0026lt;-- \"file.md\"\u003c/code\u003e) and \u003ccode\u003emeta\u003c/code\u003e per-page frontmatter, admonitions (\u003ccode\u003e!!! note\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e(c) What does NOT translate.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eMkDocs is \u003cstrong\u003esingle-page-at-a-time, server-rendered HTML\u003c/strong\u003e — no client-side graph view or SPA navigation.
